description: builders turning real NASA data into tools you can use today; our entry is live, open source and built on official NASA files.
summary:
When a Moon launch slips, can the mission still land at its site, how many days can it slip, and where else could it go? Slipday answers that for the lunar south pole, live at https://slipday.synpse.app (no sign-in).

NASA says it must keep more than one south-pole landing region open for the first crewed landing, now Artemis IV (early 2028). Slipday measures why: on the published candidate sites in NASA's nine regions, the best single region works at 26 % of landing times from 2027 to 2030 and the best three at 37 % (sunlight for a 6.25-day stay plus an illustrative 100 hours of Earth contact). IM-1, replayed: its seven-day plan had one day of slip to spare. VIPER at Mons Mouton: a one-week slip leaves 14 of 124 good landing times.

Pick a site and a date: Slipday draws the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain skyline from NASA's LOLA elevation data (5 m, 20 m or 80 m), gives a plain Yes, Not sure or No with the days of slip it can absorb, checks slope, darkness, temperature and Earth contact, and ranks what to do next. A Yes has to hold at 13 touchdown points and on more than one grid. A five-scenario mission-planner game lets students make the same calls on the same data.
details:
What it does

  • The Sun and the Earth over the real skyline. Pick a site (map, search or coordinates) and a time. The panorama shows the terrain all around you, with the Sun and Earth, their paths and a top-down compass. For the opening site (a ridge near Shackleton crater, 18 Nov 2026), the Sun is 2.3° up and 1.0° over the skyline. A 3-D view shows the shadows.
  • One decision path. The launch can slip up to 8 days if the lander touches down within 100 m of the target. All 13 touchdown points pass on 5 m terrain. A 9-day slip fails because the Earth goes behind ground 131 km away. The options are ranked: wait, or move to another site.
  • Launch windows. A missed monthly window moves the landing about a month later. January and February 2027 fail on sunlight at the opening site. Window dates are also computed from orbital geometry.
  • Compare sites. Up to four sites side by side, with one slip control for all of them, best values highlighted and CSV export.
  • Slip-day maps. How many days of slip each spot survives: the whole region to 80° S (92,416 points, every 2 km) and a close-up of the pole (14,400 points, each re-checked at 13 touchdown points).
  • Is it safe? Slope at the touchdown points against NASA's 8° crewed-lander limit (4.9° at the opening site). The chance of a safe touchdown for three lander accuracies (100 / 93.7 / 82.9 %). A battery-through-the-night calculator and a darkness check. Surface temperature from NASA's Diviner radiometer (218 K max, 44 K min at the opening site).
  • Talking to Earth. Deep Space Network station hours, and what a relay satellite on NASA's LCRNS reference orbit would add: 311 hours with the Earth alone, 336 of 336 with two relays.
  • Real missions ahead. Griffin-1, IM-4 and VIPER at Mons Mouton, and Artemis IV across NASA's nine regions, each with what a week's or a month's slip does.
  • A review-board brief. One printable page per site, with every number and assumption.
  • For everyone. A five-scenario mission-planner game, an audio mode, a glossary, and keyboard and screen-reader support.

What we found

Coarse terrain is optimistic, not noisy. Over 14 weekly dates, 452 of the 454 points where 80 m and 20 m terrain disagree are called landable on 80 m and rejected on 20 m. At the Shackleton ridge the longest darkness is 194 h on 80 m, 110 h on 20 m, and 112 h published.

How far to trust it

  • Sun and Earth directions agree with JPL Horizons to 0.00001°.
  • Sunlight agrees with the LOLA team's own illumination maps to 0.8 points on average; Earth view to 0.97.
  • A learned estimate gives an instant first answer (right 97.5 % of the time in testing) while the full check runs.
  • Every answer names the NASA grid it used.

Limits

  • No boulder data: no public NASA product covers the pole without a login.
  • The Earth-contact need is illustrative.
  • Battery defaults come from a NASA design study, not a flown lander.
  • Launch windows are a geometric approximation.
  • The 5 m grid covers two sites only.

Data and sources

  • Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA elevation — 5 m site models (two sites near Shackleton), 20 m and 80 m south-pole mosaics (LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ, LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ; Barker et al. 2023), and LDEM_75S_240M / LDEM_16 beyond 80° S.
  • Validation maps: LOLA average Sun and Earth visibility maps (AVGVISIB_85S_060M and AVGVISIB_75S_120M, 2016; method of Mazarico et al. 2011).
  • Temperature: LRO Diviner Polar Resource Product (LRO-L-DLRE-5-PRP-V2.0) and Gridded Data Record L3 (LRO-L-DLRE-5-GDR-V1.0), PDS Geosciences Node.
  • Geometry: JPL DE421 ephemeris with lunar librations; JPL Horizons for validation; DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook 810-005.
  • Landing regions and sites: NASA's nine Artemis south-pole regions (George et al., LPSC 2026, NTRS 20250011660); 78 candidate sites from Wueller et al. 2026, JGR Planets 131, e2025JE009434 (CC BY 4.0); LCRNS relay reference design.
  • Real missions: NASA CLPS press kits (IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost Mission 1) and NASA's IM-2 release of 7 Mar 2025; LROC and NSSDCA landing coordinates; ISRO Chandrayaan-3 mission page; JAXA SLIM press release of 25 Jan 2024.
  • Other: USGS/IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature; validation against Glaser et al. 2014 and 2018 and Bryant 2009 (JPL IPN Progress Report 42-176). Every site links to LROC QuickMap and NASA Moon Trek (no data taken from them).

Tools: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, jplephem), plain JavaScript and SVG. Apache-2.0.
